This article reaches a very tenuous conclusion based on what I suspect is little more than confirmation bias. It cites no evidence of any intent to discriminate in this program, which avowedly aims to reduce voter fraud (and seems, at least at first glance, reasonably tailored to do so). Indeed, the program appears to be entirely neutral on its face, merely mechanically matching suspicious instances of people with the same name voting in multiple states.

The author doesn't even consider plausible alternative explanations for a racially disparate impact (for examples, that Latinos may be more likely to share similar names, or that deliberate voter fraud could occur more often among racial minorities). Instead, it opts to jump straight to the foregone conclusion that Republicans are part of a grand conspiracy to discriminate against non-whites, published under a sensationalist heading recalling facially discriminatory laws which bear little resemblance to the one at issue here. It seems to me more about pushing a morally simple narrative of established villains to oppose and oppressed heroes to support, and less about honestly reporting the facts.

Our right to vote unhindered by these schemes is one of the most important tenets of our system. The right to vote is the subject of SIX post-Bill of Rights Constitutional Amendments. I see that the struggle is not yet over.

Let's unattenuate the starting point of this story by providing some history. This story is built upon information that should already be known.

Take a look here under 'Republicans Admit Voter Purge.'.

There's your 'conspiracy' and your prior 'confirmation.' The 'bias' is by those who would use a system that denies millions of voters the right to vote to alleviate a virtually unknown voter fraud issue, while at the same time protecting the proprietary nature of their friends' unverifiable voting machine code.

As for discriminatory intent versus disparate impact, I will be visiting those issues as stories come up. There are a few brewing.

Regardless of whether it turns out to be correct down the road, the article is jumping the gun and starting from the wrong logical premise. It sees a facially neutral practice going after voter fraud and jumps to the conclusion that those behind it are deliberately trying to keep racial minorities from voting, despite no evidence in this case. The mere fact that some Republicans have in the past used voting laws to discriminate does not automatically condemn everyone else who is either in the party or supports any law in the category.

No one has a right to cast double votes, and we should be able to talk seriously about laws preventing that sort of fraud without immediately assuming that evil, racist Republicans are at it again. It's a red herring that dangerously avoids looking at the facts, and shifts the conversation from a legal debate to a witch hunt. Is there any discriminatory practice going on, or are minorities just more likely to share similar names? Does being "tagged" under this system actually deny anyone the right to vote, or is it merely a kept record? The author doesn't even ask these questions, and doesn't seem to care about their answers.

You might even turn out to be correct that a discriminatory motive is at play here, but it's far too early to conclude as such and pronounce with as much sensationalism as possible that "Jim Crow returns."

Therefore, these laws are undemocratic.

This is a somewhat confusing post. First of all, your reasoning is highly faulty and/or unsupported (many laws which provide no benefit are still democratic; "everyone knows" is not evidence; there is no evidence of targeting racial groups in this law).

Second, and far more importantly, you're making the same mistake the author of the article makes by jumping straight to slinging insults. You're more concerned with whether the people who wrote the law are evil and hate democracy than you are with the actual merits (or lack thereof) of the law. I'm not even necessarily saying you're wrong, but that's not the place we should be starting the conversation.

That's very far from a smoking gun, my friend. There are many very uncommon crimes which are nevertheless crimes, and for good reason. Even if hardly anyone actually tries to double vote, that doesn't mean they should be allowed to do so. There's a gigantic logical gap between "I think voter fraud should be prevented" to "I hate black people and don't want them to vote." Even if the latter claim is true of the people behind these policies, you can't reasonably expect to make it with no evidence beyond differential impact.

You don't get the point. there are already mechanisms in place to detect voter fraud that work, and work very very well. That is why it does not happen. Not because no one wants to, but because no one can figure out how to do it in enough volume to sway even the closest race.
